newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Mugabe accuses critics of dividing Zimbabwe.
newsitem.headline: Mugabe accuses critics of dividing Zimbabwe.

text.p: Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe lashed out on Saturday at church critics asking his government to compensate victims of a 1980s rebellion, accusing them of digging up skeletons to divide the southern African state.
Speaking at the burial of an official of his ruling ZANU-PF party in Harare, Mugabe said Zimbabweans should treat the past as such in the interest of national unity.
"Where will we get if we keep digging up the past?...Those trying to do so are doing it in order to divide us and we must be on our guard," he said.

"They may come in religious cloak," he said in reference to a recent report by the Zimbabwe Catholic Commission for Justice and Peace. It accused an army unit deployed by Mugabe in the 1980s against an armed rebellion of murdering 3,000 innocent civilians and committing grisly atrocities.

The report, submitted to Mugabe earlier this year, calls on the government to acknowledge that its North Korean-trained Fifth Brigade committed "genocide" in Zimbabwe's Midlands and Matebeleland regions between 1982 and 1987 while trying to crush rebels aligned to the then main opposition ZAPU party.

It also urges the government to compensate surviving victims of the alleged atrocities, which many local political analysts say were intended to punish Ndebele people who formed the backbone of political opposition to Mugabe's rule.
Mugabe has consistently refused to discuss the subject or acknowledge the atrocities, saying "whatever happened during the dissidents era, happened in war".
The five-year rebellion ended in 1987 when Joshua Nkomo -- now one of Zimbabwe's two vice-presidents -- merged his ZAPU party with Mugabe's ZANU-PF.
On Saturday, Mugabe said: "These people are trying to fan factional and personal divisions among us, digging up the past so that we could end up divided on tribal and even on village lines."
"We must look forward...continue on our path and not backwards," he said, saying this was the only way to promote national reconciliation, peace and stability.

Mugabe, who assumed power 17 years ago after leading a guerrilla war for independence and black majority rule, said that in the absence of a policy of national reconciliation, the country would have been plunged into chaos.
"I would have been the first to cut Ian Smith's head off," he said of the long-serving prime minister of white-led Rhodesia -- Zimbabwe's name before independence in 1980.
